# Here we go again: Brewers advance to NLCS rematch with Dodgers

23 minutes ago

Adam McCalvy

SAN DIEGO – For the second straight year, the Brewers will play for the pennant. 

And for the second straight year, the Dodgers are standing in the way.

If this Milwaukee team really is different after winning a franchise-record 103 games in the regular season and taking down baseball’s hottest second-half team in the National League Division Series, which ended Wednesday with a 3-1 Brewers win over the Padres in Game 4 at Petco Park, then this is the time to show it. Milwaukee is moving on to the League Championship Series for the second straight season and the fifth time in franchise history. Their last three have been against the Dodgers.

Game 1 is Sunday at American Family Field, after the Dodgers finished off the Braves in four games earlier Wednesday. And if you’re wondering what’s different about this Brewers team compared to the others, it starts with this: Jacob Misiorowski will be on the mound.

The NL Cy Young Award frontrunner was in the bullpen for the start of Wednesday’s game in a sign of the urgency the Brewers carried into the night. If they could take the NLDS in four games, they would have Misiorowski primed and ready to throw the first pitch of the NLCS. But for that to become a reality, the Brewers had to rewrite the narrative that they cannot win a postseason game on the road. They had come up empty in each of their last 12 tries, tying for the longest road losing streak in the postseason in MLB history.

The last time they had won on the road in the playoffs? Game 3 of the 2018 NLCS, when they beat Walker Buehler at Dodger Stadium.

And who started for the Padres on Wednesday night? None other than Buehler.

The Brewers won the way they won games all year long, getting contributions from everywhere on the roster. 

It started with left-hander Robert Gasser, the onetime Padres prospect traded to Milwaukee in the Josh Hader deal in 2022, who’d missed most of the previous two seasons rehabbing from Tommy John surgery and didn’t crack Milwaukee’s Opening Day roster. He rose to the moment with four effective innings when it mattered most and departed with Milwaukee leading, 2-1. 

The runs came mostly from Garrett Mitchell, the former first-round Draft pick who battled four years of injuries before playing more games this season than his first four seasons combined, broke free from a 2-for-11, six-strikeout start to this series with an RBI single in third inning and a leadoff triple in the fifth that led to the go-ahead run. Jackson Chourio, the 22-year-old star in the making, lined a one-out single through a drawn-in infield for the 17th postseason RBI of his young career, passing Ryan Braun for the franchise record and matching Hall of Famer Andruw Jones for the most postseason RBIs in Major League history for a player shy of his 23rd birthday.

As of that moment, Chourio had driven in six of the Brewers’ first 12 runs in the series. 

By the time Sal Frelick’s sixth-inning sacrifice fly made it 3-1, the game belonged to the Brewers’ dynamic bullpen, starting with left-hander Aaron Ashby, whose uncle Andy pitched eight seasons for the Padres and made two All-Star teams. Ashby delivered three hitless innings to bridge the gap to Abner Uribe, facing the top of San Diego’s star-studded lineup while pitching for the fourth time in five days. He got through it, but not by much. Mitchell went all the way to Petco Park’s short center-field wall to catch what would have been a tying, two-run homer off the bat of Manny Machado for the second out of the inning, then saw second baseman Brice Turang make a tricky catch in foul ground to end the threat.

# Chourio's 2-run single with 2 outs in 9th off Miller lifts Brewers over Padres for 2-0 NLDS lead

By AP

Oct 5, 2026, 03:51 am

MILWAUKEE -- — Jackson Chourio hit a two-run single off hard-throwing Mason Miller with two outs in the ninth inning and the Milwaukee Brewers rallied past the San Diego Padres for the straight day, a 4-3 victory Sunday for a 2-0 NL Division Series lead.

 Miller entered with San Diego ahead 3-2, trying for his first six-out save since 2024. He retired the side in order in the eighth and, after a leadoff groundout in the ninth, issued his first career postseason walks to Christian Yelich and Sal Frelick.

 Andrew Vaughn flied out and pinch hitter Gary Sánchez walked on a full count.

 A night after sparking Milwaukee's comeback with a tying, two-run homer in the third inning, the 22-year-old Chourio lined a 101.3 mph fastball up the middle and past second baseman Jake Cronenworth’s attempt for a diving backhand stop. 

 The ball bounced into center field as Yelich ran across the plate. Frelick slid in head first, easily beating center fielder Jackson Merrill's throw.

 San Diego, which entered the postseason with 20 wins in its last 23 games, has back-to-back losses for the first time since Sept. 1-2. The Padres will try to keep their season alive Tuesday when the best-of-five series resumes in San Diego.

 Milwaukee is a win from a second straight NL Championship Series appearance as it chases its first World Series title.

 Chourio also made a key defensive play in the opener when France hit a potential go-ahead homer in the ninth inning only for the ball to strike a cable on the roof of American Family Field and land in Chourio's glove at the left-field warning track.

 Miller, baseball's top closer, threw 40 pitches — his most since 2023. He topped 100 mph with 18 pitches, the fastest a 103.5 mph offering that Chourio fouled.

 Milwaukee didn't have a baserunner against Padres starter Michael King until the fifth inning and matched a season high with three errors as San Diego scored a pair of unearned runs.

 With the roof open Sunday, France hit an RBI single in the first and another a run-scoring single for a 3-1 lead in the seventh after third baseman David Hamilton bobbled Fernando Tatis Jr.'s grounder for an error.

 Frelick had an RBI single in the fifth after Christian Yelich doubled.

 Milwaukee closed to 3-2 in the seventh when Garrett Mitchell scored from third as Cronenworth bobbled Hamilton's grounder and then threw past first for a double error.

MILWAUKEE -- It was center fielder Garrett Mitchell who said it last week, during a discussion about what makes this Brewers team believe it can be different than all of Milwaukee’s other seven postseason qualifiers in the preceding eight years. They all finished short of the World Series. Why should this club believe it is special?

“What feels different,” Mitchell answered, “is that we’re in it until the 27th out. This year, even down to the last out, we still have a chance. That feels different.”

- NLDS Game 3, presented by Booking.com: Tuesday, 9:30 p.m. ET, 8:30 p.m. CT, 6:30 p.m. PT on FS1/FOX Deportes/FOX One

Which brings us to the bottom of the ninth inning of Game 2 of the National League Division Series on Sunday at American Family Field, a dud until it wasn’t, and a 4-3 walk-off win over the Padres on Jackson Chourio’s two-out, two-strike single off elite closer Mason Miller.

- Brewers Postseason Tickets are on sale now!

It was the third walk-off win in the postseason in Brewers history, with Mike Moustakas’ base hit to end 2018 NLDS Game 1 against the Rockies and Nyjer Morgan’s dribbler up the middle in the 10th inning of 2011 NLDS Game 5 against the D-backs to give Milwaukee its first postseason series victory in 29 years.

The Milwaukee faithful celebrated loudly that day.

They did it all over again on Sunday.

MILWAUKEE -- Matt Erickson called it.

Hours before Ty France's controversial fly ball -- a potential go-ahead home run in the ninth inning that struck a cable on the roof of American Family Field -- Erickson, the Brewers' third-base coach, took part in the usual exchange of lineup cards at home plate.

- NLDS Game 3, presented by Booking.com: Tuesday, 9:30 p.m. ET, 8:30 p.m. CT, 6:30 p.m. PT on FS1/FOX Deportes/FOX One

Before Game 1 of the National League Division Series -- an eventual 3-2 Brewers victory-- Erickson and Padres manager Craig Stammen spoke with the umpiring crew about the ballpark’s ground rules. At the end of their discussion, home-plate ump Nick Mahrley clarified what would happen if a ball were to hit the cables attached to the roof.

A day later, the FS1 broadcast showed some remarkably prescient footage of the meeting.

“If it hits fair,” Mahrley says, “wherever it comes down, whatever happens, that’s what we’ve got.”

- Padres Postseason tickets on sale now!

To which Stammen even asked for a clarification:

“It can be caught?” he said.

“Yes,” another of the umpires responded.

- Brewers Postseason Tickets are on sale now!

It was at that point that Erickson chimed in:

“I haven’t seen that here in six years,” he said. “So it’ll happen tonight.”

Sure enough, France’s bid at a go-ahead two-run homer struck the cable, and Jackson Chourio settled under it to make the catch for the second out of the ninth inning. Where would the ball have otherwise landed? That might be the subject of debate for years to come.

But there was no debating the ruling.

"I've been out there quite a few times for lineup card exchanges, and there's some generalities of the ground rules,” Erickson said late Saturday night. “Very rarely is the roof talked about. And tonight, it was clearly explained -- almost identical to the play that happened.

“So, credit to the umpires for knowing what was at stake and letting everybody know the rules."

Padres lose 2026 NLDS to Brewers

# Padres left wondering what could have been after NLDS exit: 'It stings'

October 8th, 2026

AJ Cassavell

SAN DIEGO -- Every postseason exit hurts. They may hurt for different reasons. They all hurt.

This one, most of all, is going to hurt because of what could have been.

The Padres and Brewers staged an epic of a National League Division Series. The margins were thin. Agonizingly thin. A potential go-ahead home run off a cable on the roof in Milwaukee in Game 1. A Jackson Chourio line drive just beyond the outstretched glove of Jake Cronenworth in Game 2.

And maybe the cruelest of all: A potential game-tying, season-saving, bedlam-inducing home run from the bat of Manny Machado, taken away at the wall by Brewers center fielder Garrett Mitchell in Game 4.

Just like that, the Padres’ season was over. They dropped Game 4 of the NLDS to Milwaukee, 3-1, on Wednesday night at Petco Park. They lost the series by the same tally. So easily, it could have been different.

“It burns," said Machado. “It's pain. This team, we fought all year, dealt with a lot as a group. Overcame a lot. It stings right now, for sure. But at the same time, proud of these guys, what they've accomplished, what they've done, what we did this year -- a lot of great things. 

“Unfortunate. It just didn't go our way. But take the punch, and enjoy the ride that we had.”

This wasn’t 2024, when the Padres came apart in the two biggest games of their season. It wasn’t ‘25, when they fizzled, never quite reaching the gear you thought they might. These Padres could have beaten the Brewers. For years, San Diegans will swear that they should have.

They did not. For the first time in 111 years, a postseason series featured two teams that were never separated by more than two runs in any game. And the Padres came out on the losing end of it.

“It was a heavyweight battle,” said France. “They were the best team in baseball for a reason, and … we went punch-for-punch with them.”

The Padres weren’t making any excuses afterward, fully crediting the 103-win Brewers as deserving winners. Still, France and so many others will always believe, deep down, that his Game 1 fly ball would have been a go-ahead home run, had it not struck that cable. On Wednesday night, Brewers manager Pat Murphy wasn’t disputing that.

“The Padres, they’re a great team,” Murphy said. “They could have won it all, but that's just the postseason. The ball doesn't bounce your way. [Legendary late Brewers broadcaster Bob] Uecker knocks that ball down out of the rafters. And it's a different series. Chourio gets the hit off Miller, and it's a different series.

“So believe me, that team right there can beat anybody in baseball. I'm just grateful we got through.”

With time, the disappointment will be complemented by an appreciation that the Padres got here in the first place. Three games below .500 in late July, they stormed into the postseason with a scorching hot finish, then played six deeply memorable postseason games.

And yet, the wait goes on. There’s never been an era of Padres baseball quite like this one. They’ve reached the postseason in three straight years and five of seven. But this era still lacks its crowning achievement -- the first World Series title in franchise history.

“A lot to be proud of this year,” said manager Craig Stammen. “A lot to go home and say: ‘Yeah, we did a pretty good job.’ But also, we're not satisfied. We're not satisfied until we finally bring that championship to San Diego. But this year made us one step closer.”

An offseason full of questions lies ahead. The futures of Adrian Morejon, Ty France and Michael King are chief among those questions. In the aftermath of Wednesday’s defeat, all three expressed a desire to return.

# Jackson Chourio’s two-run walk-off single off of Mason Miller lifts Brewers to NLDS Game 2 victory

Brewers outfielder Jackson Chourio hit a game-winning two-run single off with two outs in the ninth inning to lead his team to a Game 2 victory over the Padres. Kayla Wolf/AP Photo/Kayla Wolf

MILWAUKEE — Jackson Chourio says his knack for coming through in clutch situations stems from one instance when he failed to deliver during his rookie year.

Just about every Brewers opponent has been paying for that ever since, as baseball’s best closer now knows.

Chourio hit a two-run single off hard-throwing Mason Miller with two outs in the ninth inning as the Brewers rallied past the San Diego Padres for the second straight day, a 4-3 victory Sunday for a 2-0 NL Division Series lead.

“I think it’s probably in the top three of the special moments I’ve had in my career,” Chourio said through interpreter Daniel de Mondesert.

The fact Chourio didn’t automatically rank it atop the list speaks volumes about all the memorable moments the 22-year-old already has produced in his first three seasons. Chourio said his drive to deliver in these moments intensified after he struck out against Andrés Muñoz, ending a loss to Seattle early in his rookie year.

“At that point, everything turned for me,” Chourio said. “I told myself I was never going to make the last out. I’d dedicate myself to fighting and doing whatever I could for the team and not having that feeling again from that specific game.”

San Diego, which entered the postseason with 20 wins in its last 23 games, headed home for Game 3 of the best-of-five series on Tuesday following its first back-to-back losses since Sept. 1-2.

Milwaukee rallied from 2-0 deficits on consecutive days by beating the Padres’ bullpen. William Contreras hit a tiebreaking homer in the seventh inning against Adrian Morejon on Saturday.

“It’s a big challenge,” Padres manager Craig Stammen said. “They’re a great team. You saw how hard they battle us here in Milwaukee. But we like where we are when we play at home.”

Michael King retired his first 14 batters as the Padres went ahead 2-0, and they led 3-2 when Miller entered trying for his first six-out save since 2024.

The two-time All-Star closer retired the side in order in the eighth. After a leadoff groundout in the ninth, Miller issued his first career postseason walks to Christian Yelich and Sal Frelick.

Andrew Vaughn flied out and pinch hitter Gary Sánchez walked, taking six straight pitches.

That brought Chourio to the plate, one day after he sparked a 4-3 comeback victory with a tying, two-run homer in the third inning.

“Watching those at-bats beforehand, I knew that he was a little bit erratic,” Chourio said. “He was throwing some balls. I knew that he was going to come at me with the fastball at some point, so mentally I was just making sure that I was prepared for that.”

Chourio connected on a 2-2 pitch, lining a 101.3 mile-per-hour fastball up the middle and past second baseman Jake Cronenworth’s attempt for a diving backhand stop. Cronenworth believed he was inches away from making the play.

“He smashed it, but I thought I got a good jump on it,” Cronenworth said.

The ball bounced into center field as Yelich ran across the plate. Frelick slid in head first, easily beating center fielder Jackson Merrill’s throw.

Miller threw a season-high 40 pitches — his most since 2023 — but said after the game that didn’t impact him. He topped 100 mph with 18 pitches, the fastest a 103.5 mph offering that Chourio fouled.

“I didn’t do my job today, so instead of being here with a win and a series tie, we’re in a hole,” Miller said.

# Contreras comes up clutch as Crew captures Game 1 win in NLDS

By Adam McCalvy | 15 minutes ago

This browser does not support the video element.

MILWAUKEE -- William Contreras didn’t have to hustle down the line on this one.

The Brewers were happy to watch him trot.

The All-Star catcher who was benched for failing to hustle during the final week of the regular season, playing for the team that won 103 games in the regular season while hitting the fewest home runs in the National League, showed that the start of the postseason means a clean slate when Contreras connected for a go-ahead solo shot in the seventh inning of the Brewers’ 3-2 win over the Padres in Game 1 of the NL Division Series on Saturday night at American Family Field.

“These are the type of games that I like,” Contreras said through an interpreter. “I like playing in these intense games. Fortunately, we were able to play our brand of baseball both offensively and defensively. So, this is the first of many to come.”

With one on and one out in the top of the ninth against closer Trevor Megill, Ty France hit a deep drive to left field that struck the cables on the roof of the ballpark. Was it headed fair or foul? Impossible to tell. But there was at least a decent chance it would have left the yard.

Instead, the ball settled in the glove of left fielder Jackson Chourio and was ruled an out upon replay review. And a batter later, the Brewers had secured the win.

This browser does not support the video element.

“At first, it was, ‘Oh, crap.’ And then the home-plate umpire came up and said it was live no matter what,” Megill said. “Four years in this stadium, I’ve never seen that before. Just glad it worked in our favor.”

The Brewers got four shaky innings from ace starter Jacob Misiorowski and won anyway. They got a tying, two-run home run from Chourio off Padres starter Robbie Ray in the third inning that made Chourio, all of 22 years old, Milwaukee’s all-time leader with five postseason home runs. Then the Brewers got a go-ahead shot from Contreras off the Padres’ ace setup man, Adrian Morejon, a left-hander who yielded four home runs in 86 innings during the regular season.

It was a satisfying trot around the bases for Contreras, who means so much to the Brewers’ vaunted run prevention unit as Major League Baseball’s leader in innings behind the plate during the regular season, and who led the Majors and set a Brewers record this season with 89 RBIs while playing catcher.

Contreras is not the type of man who likes to have his commitment questioned, but that’s what occurred during the Brewers’ final road series of the regular season in Philadelphia, on the night the Brewers secured the first 100-win season in club history. After Contreras didn’t hustle to first base on a bouncer that Phillies shortstop Trea Turner bobbled, Brewers manager Pat Murphy pulled Contreras in favor of a pinch-hitter. It was meant to send a message to the team that the high standards required to contend every season on a tight budget apply to everyone, even three-time All-Stars.

Contreras got the message. When he grounded out in his first at-bat the following night, he dived headfirst into first base. Murphy smiled in the dugout. He later called it "beautiful."

Not as beautiful, perhaps, as the fly ball that left the game in the hands of the Brewers’ well-rested bullpen. Left-hander DL Hall, who rose to a high-leverage role late in the regular season, escaped a bases-loaded jam in the seventh inning and secured the first two outs of the eighth before turning it over, with the tying runner on third base, to Megill, who struck out Fernando Tatis Jr. to preserve the lead and then worked around the wacky France flyout in the ninth to give the Brewers a 1-0 lead in the series.

# Padres avoid elimination, beat Brewers 4-3 in NLDS Game 3 with Cronenworth's HR, King's relief

By AP

Updated: Oct 7, 2026, 01:37 am

SAN DIEGO -- — Jake Cronenworth hit a tiebreaking homer, Game 2 starter Michael King pitched the final two innings on one day of rest and the San Diego Padres avoided playoff elimination with a 4-3 victory over the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of their NL Division Series on Tuesday night.

 Xander Bogaerts turned a game-ending double play at shortstop for the Padres, who trimmed Milwaukee’s lead in the best-of-five series to 2-1 with a tense, back-and-forth victory over the MLB-best Brewers.

 Game 4 is Wednesday night at Petco Park. If necessary, Game 5 will be back in Milwaukee on Friday.

 Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado drove in early runs for the Padres, but their bullpen didn’t have star closer Mason Miller, who went on the paternity list about 45 minutes before the first pitch. King stepped up after pitching five innings just two days ago and finished it off — but only after a thrilling ninth.

 The right-hander retired four of his first five batters, but William Contreras and Brice Turang drew one-out walks in the ninth. Christian Yelich then cracked a 107 mph line drive up the middle, where Bogaerts went down to his knees to field it on a short hop and scampered to touch second base before throwing out Yelich at first to end it.

 King earned his first save since 2023, his first in the postseason and his first for the Padres.

 Contreras homered and had three hits for the Brewers, who lost their 12th consecutive postseason road game dating to the 2018 National League Championship Series.

 Yelich even got his first playoff RBI since 2018 with a seventh-inning single, but Milwaukee fell behind early and never led, leaving 11 runners on base.

Padres back on track

 The Padres had won 19 of 22 and swept the Cubs out of the Wild Card Series before losing two straight heartbreakers in Milwaukee last weekend, but they are fighting to stay with the majors’ best regular-season team.

 The clubs have played three consecutive one-run games in this NLDS, all decided by late-game execution — and this time, the Padres came through.

 They were also bailed out by King, largely a reliever early in his major league career with the Yankees. This game was just his third relief appearance in three seasons with San Diego — and according to OptaStats, he is the first pitcher to start a postseason game and then earn a two-inning save within the next two days since saves became an official statistic in 1969.

Back-and-forth game

 Neither starter excelled on a tense, uncommonly hot October night in downtown San Diego. Nick Pivetta yielded two runs and five hits while pitching into the fifth for the Padres, and Dustin May got pulled abruptly with a 1-0 count on Bogaerts and a runner on in the fourth.

 Samad Taylor and Jackson Merrill put San Diego ahead in the third when both singled, stole second and scored. Contreras answered with his second homer of the series, adding a theatrical trot around the bases.

 Cooper Pratt tied it right after Pivetta’s exit when Dustin Harris couldn’t throw him out on Jackson Chourio’s 242-foot sacrifice fly. It was the fifth RBI of the series for the 22-year-old Chourio and his 16th in 15 career postseason games, already tying Ryan Braun for the franchise record.

 Cronenworth lined JoJo Romero’s first pitch of the fifth over the wall in right for only his second hit of the postseason.

 Bogaerts then singled in the sixth, advanced on a wild pitch and scored when Pratt bounced his throw from shortstop for an error after Miguel Andujar’s broken bat came flying toward him along with the grounder.

results.title: Padres avoid elimination after 4-3 win over Brewers in NLDS Game 3
results.text:
Padres avoid elimination after 4-3 win over Brewers in NLDS Game 3 

# Padres avoid elimination after 4-3 win over Brewers in NLDS Game 3 

Game 4 is Wednesday night at Petco Park. If necessary, Game 5 will be back in Milwaukee on Friday.

The San Diego Padres' Jake Cronenworth rounds the bases after his home run against the Milwaukee Brewers during the fifth inning in Game 3 of the National League Division Series at Petco Park on Tuesday. Meg McLaughlin / The San Diego Union-Tribune / Getty Images

Oct. 7, 2026, 1:53 AM EDT / Source: The Associated Press

By The Associated Press

SAN DIEGO — Jake Cronenworth hit a tiebreaking homer, Game 2 starter Michael King pitched the final two innings on one day of rest and the San Diego Padres avoided playoff elimination with a 4-3 victory over the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of their NL Division Series on Tuesday night.

Xander Bogaerts turned a game-ending double play at shortstop for the Padres, who trimmed Milwaukee’s lead in the best-of-five series to 2-1 with a tense, back-and-forth victory over the MLB-best Brewers.

Game 4 is Wednesday night at Petco Park. If necessary, Game 5 will be back in Milwaukee on Friday.

Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado drove in early runs for the Padres, but their bullpen didn’t have star closer Mason Miller, who went on the paternity list about 45 minutes before the first pitch. King stepped up after pitching five innings just two days ago and finished it off — but only after a thrilling ninth.

The right-hander retired four of his first five batters, but William Contreras and Brice Turang drew one-out walks in the ninth. Christian Yelich then cracked a 107 mph line drive up the middle, where Bogaerts went down to his knees to field it on a short hop and scampered to touch second base before throwing out Yelich at first to end it.

King earned his first save since 2023, his first in the postseason and his first for the Padres.

Contreras homered and had three hits for the Brewers, who lost their 12th consecutive postseason road game dating to the 2018 National League Championship Series.

Yelich even got his first playoff RBI since 2018 with a seventh-inning single, but Milwaukee fell behind early and never led, leaving 11 runners on base.

## Padres back on track

The Padres had won 19 of 22 and swept the Cubs out of the Wild Card Series before losing two straight heartbreakers in Milwaukee last weekend, but they are fighting to stay with the majors’ best regular-season team.

The clubs have played three consecutive one-run games in this NLDS, all decided by late-game execution — and this time, the Padres came through.

They were also bailed out by King, largely a reliever early in his major league career with the Yankees. This game was just his third relief appearance in three seasons with San Diego — and according to OptaStats, he is the first pitcher to start a postseason game and then earn a two-inning save within the next two days since saves became an official statistic in 1969.

## Back-and-forth game

Neither starter excelled on a tense, uncommonly hot October night in downtown San Diego. Nick Pivetta yielded two runs and five hits while pitching into the fifth for the Padres, and Dustin May got pulled abruptly with a 1-0 count on Bogaerts and a runner on in the fourth.

Samad Taylor and Jackson Merrill put San Diego ahead in the third when both singled, stole second and scored. Contreras answered with his second homer of the series, adding a theatrical trot around the bases.

Cooper Pratt tied it right after Pivetta’s exit when Dustin Harris couldn’t throw him out on Jackson Chourio’s 242-foot sacrifice fly. It was the fifth RBI of the series for the 22-year-old Chourio and his 16th in 15 career postseason games, already tying Ryan Braun for the franchise record.

Cronenworth lined JoJo Romero’s first pitch of the fifth over the wall in right for only his second hit of the postseason.
